title: How We Change Together
coreMove: Design tiny behaviors for a group by shrinking the ask, anchoring it to a shared routine, and celebrating others' wins out loud so the wiring spreads through the relationship rather than through pressure.

exampleSpecs.domain: a charge nurse trying to get her night shift to actually use the new handoff checklist without turning huddle into a lecture
exampleSpecs.audience: a charge nurse who inherited a team that has quietly ignored three previous process rollouts
exampleSpecs.stakes: patient safety on a unit where missed medication reconciliations have already triggered one near-miss this quarter
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she shrinks the ask to a single line on the checklist, anchors it to the moment the outgoing nurse hangs up the COW, and notices that praising the first nurse who did it in front of the others made the second nurse do it unprompted — without her ever invoking discipline or duty

exampleSpecs.domain: a father coaching his ten-year-old to put on a bike helmet without daily nagging
exampleSpecs.audience: a parent whose previous sticker chart system collapsed within a week
exampleSpecs.stakes: a busy suburban street and a kid who has started biking to a friend's house alone
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the father drops the lecture, agrees with the kid that the new behavior is just clipping the chinstrap once after grabbing the handlebars, and celebrates the click out loud with a high-five — letting the child feel competent rather than corrected

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school orchestra director getting forty teenagers to actually take instruments home for weekend practice
exampleSpecs.audience: a music teacher whose 'practice 30 minutes a day' assignment is being ignored by two thirds of the section
exampleSpecs.stakes: spring concert is six weeks out and the second violins cannot get through the Dvorak passage
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the before shows him assigning thirty minutes and shaming the empty practice logs; the after shows him asking each kid to open the case and play one note after they get home from school, and to text a thumbs-up to a partner — the partner texting back is the celebration that does the wiring

exampleSpecs.domain: two roommates trying to keep a shared kitchen from devolving by Friday
exampleSpecs.audience: a pair of twenty-somethings sharing a small Brooklyn apartment, neither of whom wants to be the nag
exampleSpecs.stakes: a friendship that has survived three years and a lease that just got renewed
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: they agree that after either of them sets down a dirty dish, they wipe one square inch of counter, and whoever sees it says 'nice' — the warmth in the small acknowledgment is the load-bearing piece, not the cleanliness itself

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional manager rolling out a new safety walk to twelve warehouse supervisors who quietly resent corporate initiatives
exampleSpecs.audience: a regional manager who has watched two prior 'culture' rollouts die
exampleSpecs.stakes: an OSHA inspection in two months and a workforce that has stopped trusting that any new program will outlast the quarter
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after the rollout works, she walks back through what she actually did differently — she did not mandate the full walk, she asked supervisors to check one rack after their morning coffee and to text the group chat a thumbs-up, and she replied to every single text within an hour for the first two weeks; the celebration was hers, given to them

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospice social worker helping a grieving spouse build a single morning ritual that does not collapse under the weight of the loss
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinician sitting with a 71-year-old widower three weeks after his wife's death
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether this man eats breakfast at all this month, and whether the small rhythm of a day comes back before the grief calcifies into immobility
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the social worker resists prescribing a routine and instead asks the man what his wife used to do first; she helps him anchor 'fill the kettle' to waking up, and she calls the next morning only to hear him say he did it, then says 'good' and lets that one word land — change happening through being witnessed, not through being instructed
